strengths: Addresses a timely and under-explored problem: the 'frozen world' assumption in LRM evaluation and the need for interruptibility / dynamic-context handling. The framing around time-constrained and update-driven interruptions is conceptually clear and practically motivated (assistive programming, long-running reasoning).

Introduces a formal problem setup distinguishing hard interrupts (end-thinking / force-answer), soft interrupts (speedup), and update-driven interrupts, with an interruption-conditioned accuracy A_i(X) and length L_i(X) that extend static accuracy to dynamic settings.

Identifies and characterizes three novel and memorable failure modes—reasoning leakage, panic, and self-doubt—with both quantitative evidence (e.g., up to 10x longer answers after hard interrupt in Figure 1b/Figure 2 bottom; up to ~80-90% of new errors attributable to panic in Figure 1b) and qualitative examples in Appendix C (e.g., Listing C.1, C.2, C.3).

The scaling ablation (Qwen3-1.7B/8B/32B) and the assistant-turn vs user-turn comparison add useful dimensions, and the observation that small models exhibit post-hoc reasoning (Listing C.2) is an interesting finding.
Reproducibility materials are relatively thorough: full prompt templates (Appendix B), dataset construction pipeline and generation prompts (Appendix D), and an LLM-use disclosure (Appendix A).
Includes a dedicated limitations section (Section 7) that honestly discusses task diversity, single well-defined interruptions, and a small model set.
weaknesses: Presentation quality is weak for a top venue: multiple malformed LaTeX/math expressions (e.g., the two-stage inference equations in Section 3.1 and the hard-interrupt mapping '(r_X')=\emptyset,\,a')' are broken), and a stray '</eos></update></update>' token appears in the body of Section 6.1. Many figures are low-resolution and difficult to read, making it hard to verify the quantitative claims (e.g., Figures 2, 3, 6, 7).

Statistical strength is limited: only AIME uses 16 trials; GSM8K, MATH-500, and LiveCodeBench use a single run. Given the claimed up-to-60% drops and the emphasis on late-interruption fragility, single-run accuracy curves are insufficient to support several headline claims, and bootstrapped CIs on a single run do not capture run-to-run variance.

The failure-mode quantification (panic, self-doubt) appears ad-hoc/subjective; the classification procedure and the criteria for attributing a fraction of errors to 'panic' vs other causes are not rigorously specified, making the '80-90% of errors' claims hard to verify or reproduce.

The 'prompt guidance' remedy (appending text in the model's own voice asserting the update is verified) is a somewhat artificial intervention, and the claim that it 'fully resolves' self-doubt on GSM8K/MATH-500 is strong relative to the evidence; the fix also conflates the phenomenon (self-doubt) with a prompt-engineering workaround rather than establishing a robust capability.

The model set is limited to small open-weight models (Qwen3-8B, GPT-OSS-20B, Magistral-Small-1.2, plus Qwen3 scaling); claims about 'state-of-the-art LRMs' would be stronger with frontier proprietary models included. Generalization beyond these architectures/scales is uncertain.

There is a slight framing tension: the hard-interrupt results are described as 'approximately anytime' graceful degradation, yet the abstract/contributions emphasize severe fragility. The paper would benefit from reconciling these and clarifying which settings genuinely violate anytime behavior.

Some dataset augmentations in Appendix D appear loosely controlled (e.g., changes that alter difficulty or solver intent rather than cleanly inverting a single specification), which could confound the 'necessary update' requirement a*(q) != a*(q,u) and the interpretation of the accuracy drops.

strengths: The paper asks a timely and practically relevant question: how large reasoning models behave when their reasoning is interrupted or their context changes mid-inference, challenging the standard frozen-world evaluation assumption.

It conducts a broad empirical sweep across math and coding benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH500, AIME24/25, LiveCodeBench-v6), multiple interruption positions, and several models, and reports both accuracy and output-length effects.
It identifies concrete and qualitatively illustrated failure modes—reasoning leakage, panic, and self-doubt—that are useful phenomena for the community to study further.
The framework formalizes interruption-conditioned accuracy and post-interruption length, and the ablation studies (model scale, assistant-turn vs. user-turn) add useful empirical detail.
The authors include a limitations section and disclose LLM assistance, which is appropriate.
weaknesses: The central failure-mode claims are not rigorously supported. The paper reports that >90% of speedup errors are due to panic and ~80% of update-driven errors stem from self-doubt, but it never defines an operational criterion or annotation protocol for attributing errors to these modes, nor reports inter-annotator agreement. This makes the headline claims qualitative rather than quantitative.

The evaluation covers only three main open-weight models (Qwen3-8B, GPT-OSS-20B, Magistral-Small-1.2) plus Qwen3 scales, omitting leading LRMs such as OpenAI o1/o3, Gemini, and DeepSeek-R1. Claims about 'state-of-the-art LRMs' are therefore overstated.

Interruption positions are defined as fractions of the oracle full reasoning trace length R_T (0.1,...,0.9). This requires knowing the eventual full trace in advance and does not model exogenous, unpredictable interruptions in real deployments. The design may bias results, especially for late interruptions at 0.9R_T.

The update-driven math benchmark is constructed by first modifying a problem and then supplying an update that restores the original problem. This may induce 'self-doubt' by construction, since the model initially reasons toward a different answer. It is unclear how well the findings transfer to updates that change the goal to a new answer.

The proposed 'prompt guidance' is a hand-crafted string inserted in the model's voice ('I have verified that the update is provided by the user...'). It is a prompt-engineering trick rather than a principled method, and the paper overclaims by saying it 'fully resolves' self-doubt on GSM8K/MATH500. No comparison to simple restart-from-scratch or other baselines is provided.

The coding evaluation under update-driven interruptions is underspecified. It is not clear how augmented coding problems are evaluated, whether official tests are used, how updated test cases are executed, or how partial correctness is handled. This is a major reproducibility gap.

The paper claims a 'new public dataset and benchmark' but provides no link, accession, or release details in the manuscript. Dataset construction uses GPT-5 and manual verification, but counts, annotation protocol, and quality-control statistics are missing.

Presentation quality is poor in places: inconsistent notation (r_{|X}, r_{.X}, r_{X:}), missing parentheses in equations, typos such as 'Groud Truth' and 'tfrac', and an inconsistent problem statement in Appendix C.3 (m-n vs. m+n). These issues hinder clarity.

Statistical rigor is limited: most benchmarks use a single run (except AIME with 16 trials), and there are no significance tests for many key comparisons. Bootstrapped confidence intervals are mentioned but not always shown or used to support claims.

Novelty is incremental relative to prior work on budget forcing and efficient reasoning, which already studies hard cutoffs and overthinking. The paper's main contribution is empirical characterization rather than a new method or theory.

strengths: Timely and novel problem framing: the paper challenges the pervasive 'frozen world' assumption in LRM evaluation and formalizes interruptible reasoning under two realistic regimes (time-constrained hard/soft interrupts and update-driven context changes).

Clear and reusable evaluation design: a two-stage inference formalization, interruption-conditioned accuracy A_i(X), length L_i(X), and relative interrupt positions (X in {0.1,...,0.9}·R_T) that normalize across models with very different trace lengths.
Identification of several genuinely interesting failure modes (reasoning leakage, panic, self-doubt) with concrete qualitative examples (Listings C.1-C.3) and quantitative plots (Figs. 1-3).

Actionable insight beyond diagnosis: the 'prompt guidance' postfix substantially mitigates self-doubt on GSM8K/MATH-500, and the assistant-turn vs user-turn comparison (Fig. 8) offers practical guidance for deployment.
Ablations add value, including model-scale analysis (Fig. 7) showing increased leakage in small models and a robustness scaling limit, plus an update+speedup combination study (Figs. E.2-E.3).
Good presentation, clear figures, an explicit limitations section, and an LLM-use disclosure (Appendix A).
weaknesses: The central failure-mode statistics (e.g., 'over 90% of new errors under speedup arise from panic', '~80% of update-driven errors stem from self-doubt', 'up to 80% of performance loss attributable to panic') are stated without a described, reproducible attribution/labeling protocol. How errors are classified as panic vs. self-doubt vs. other causes is not specified, weakening the soundness of a headline claim.

Evaluation breadth and statistical power are limited: only three main models, and a single run for GSM8K, MATH-500, and LiveCodeBench (16 runs only for AIME). Many reported differences (e.g., Magistral on GSM8K at 0.9, coding task trends) are small and may fall within run-to-run variance.

Headline numbers ('up to 60%' drops, 'up to 10x' longer answers) appear to be cherry-picked extremes rather than systematic effect sizes (means/medians with CIs); the paper would be stronger with aggregate measures of degradation.

The update-driven dataset is generated by GPT-5 and 'manually verified', but the paper does not report dataset size, verification criteria, inter-annotator agreement, or the fraction of replaced items, which limits confidence in and reproducibility of the augmented benchmarks.

The 'anytime behavior' framing is somewhat loose: the paper itself reports non-monotonic cases (e.g., Magistral on AIME 0.3, late coding interrupts improving performance), yet the anytime claim is presented as the general pattern without a rigorous test of monotonicity.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed: prompts and hyperparameters are given, but the promised public benchmark/dataset and code are not clearly referenced with a link, and results depend on model-specific prompt/format handling (e.g., Qwen3 single thinking block) that may not transfer.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important gap: evaluating large reasoning models under mid-inference interruptions and dynamic context updates, directly challenging the standard frozen-world evaluation assumption.

Provides a comprehensive and reusable evaluation suite/protocol across hard interrupts, soft speedup interrupts, and update-driven interruptions on math and coding benchmarks, with multiple models, scales, interruption schedules, and prompt variants.

Identifies and quantifies three recurring failure modes—reasoning leakage, panic, and self-doubt—that are not captured by static evaluations and are supported by qualitative examples, length/accuracy analyses, and error-rate breakdowns.

Reproducibility is relatively strong: code/data are released, prompts and dataset construction are detailed, updates are manually verified, and a memorization check is included to validate the augmented math problems.

The experimental coverage is extensive: main-paper models plus additional open-weight models in the appendix, model-scale ablations, assistant- vs user-turn interruption, sentence-level and absolute-token interruption, Chain-of-Draft baseline, and panic-threshold sensitivity.
The limitations section is honest and well scoped, acknowledging single-event interruptions, the open-weight focus, the weak proprietary-API proxy, and the lack of a trained mitigation method.
The paper provides useful conceptual framing for future work: interruptibility as a distinct capability, with failure modes that could inform interruption-aware training and evaluation.
weaknesses: The main interruption protocol defines cut points relative to the eventual full reasoning trace length, which is not observable in real-time interruption settings. Although sentence-level and absolute-token ablations are provided, the main results rely on this oracle-normalized timing, limiting direct practical interpretation.

Most datasets are evaluated with a single run, and only AIME uses 16 trials; while bootstrapped confidence intervals are reported, some comparative claims (especially around late-stage drops and error attribution) may still be noisy and would benefit from more repeated runs.

Failure-mode labels depend on heuristics and an LLM classifier: panic is defined by a <1% remaining-context threshold after speedup, and self-doubt is classified with GPT-5. The paper reports human agreement on 50 samples each, but the causal attribution of performance loss to panic/self-doubt remains correlational rather than interventional.

Closed-source state-of-the-art models are not natively evaluated because APIs do not expose editable reasoning traces. The GPT-5.4-Mini proxy is explicitly acknowledged as unfaithful, which weakens claims about the broader class of frontier proprietary LRMs.

The proposed prompt-guidance mitigation is a short postfix that asserts the update is verified by the user; it improves easy-task performance but does not solve harder settings, and its interaction with model trust/instruction-following is not deeply analyzed. No training-based or principled mitigation is proposed.
Update-driven datasets are generated with GPT-5 and manually verified, but the benchmark may still inherit generation artifacts or coverage biases despite the >80% acceptance rate and manual review.
The study only considers single, well-defined interruptions; multiple, noisy, or adversarial interruptions are left to future work, which limits claims about richer interactive deployments.

strengths: The paper frames a genuinely novel and practically motivated evaluation axis—interruptible reasoning—and formalizes it cleanly (hard/soft time-constrained interrupts and update-driven interrupts) with a precise two-stage inference notation and interruption-conditioned accuracy/length metrics.

The empirical scope is substantial: 5+ model families across 4 benchmarks, multiple interruption points, several granularities (character-, sentence-, and absolute-token-level), model-scaling ablations, assistant- vs user-turn injection, prompt-paraphrase controls, and an inference-control baseline (Chain of Draft).

Reproducibility is reasonably strong: code and data are released under MIT, all prompts/hyperparameters are documented in the appendix, and the authors disclose LLM assistance in preparing the manuscript.

The benchmark is sensibly validated—the 'augmented-problem-without-interruption' control (near-zero accuracy against original answers) is a good check against memorization—and the failure-mode heuristics are human-validated (90% for panic, 88% for self-doubt).
Limitations are discussed honestly and specifically (single well-defined interrupts, open-weight-only, no mitigation method), which is appropriate for an analysis paper.
weaknesses: The 'self-doubt' pathology is largely eliminated by a short, training-free prompt-guidance postfix that 'fully resolves' it on GSM8K/MATH-500. If a trivial rephrasing removes the failure, the phenomenon looks more like prompt-sensitivity of the assistant-turn injection than a fundamental, distinct capability gap, which undercuts the paper's headline error taxonomy.

The update-driven construction (reason p' for X% of the trace, then supply u that reverts to the original p) places the model in a self-contradictory context. Questioning a contradictory mid-stream instruction is arguably reasonable behavior, so labeling this as a 'failure mode' is a stretch and may confound the analysis with instruction-following quirks.

Novelty is limited relative to prior work. Reasoning leakage and premature/over-long reasoning are already documented in budget-forcing (Muennighoff et al., 2025) and missing-premise overthinking (Fan et al., 2025); the paper's stated distinction from s1 is thin, and no new method or training intervention is proposed.

Several headline quantitative claims ('up to 60%', 'over 90% of new errors arise from panic', '~80% of update-driven errors stem from self-doubt') are asserted rather than demonstrated in the main text, and the attributions rest on an LLM-based classifier plus a heuristic threshold, making the central causal claims hard to verify.

The 'panic' heuristic (<1% of remaining context after a soft interrupt) and the 'leakage' measure (longer final-answer strings vs. an oracle) conflate answer verbosity/detail with genuine reasoning spillover, so the taxonomy partly operationalizes its own definitions.

Presentation is weak and at times obstructive: recurring typos ('argentic' for agentic, 'Nematron' for Nemotron, 'tfrac'/'frac', 'Inftythink'), a visibly broken citation ('(2025Sci.Proceedings...'), and figure/text inconsistencies that make the results difficult to check.

Interruptions are injected inside the assistant turn because user-turn interruptions break several models; the authors acknowledge this is unnatural and not uniformly supported, limiting external validity for real interactive deployments.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important gap: static frozen-world evaluation of LRMs versus dynamic interruptions and mid-inference updates.
Defines a clear formal setup for hard, soft, and update-driven interruptions, with correctness A_i(X) and post-interrupt length L_i(X) as evaluation metrics.
Introduces a public benchmark with human-verified updates, standardized protocols, released code/data, and reproducible implementation details.
Provides broad empirical coverage across math and coding benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH-500, AIME-24/25, LiveCodeBench-v6), multiple open-weight models, interruption positions, and several ablations.
Identifies and quantifies three novel and practically relevant failure modes: reasoning leakage, panic, and self-doubt, supported by qualitative examples and error-rate analyses.
Includes useful robustness checks: sentence-level and absolute-token interruptions, model scaling, Chain-of-Draft baseline, prompt-guidance paraphrase, and a memorization check.
Reproducibility is strong: open models, vLLM, explicit prompts, dataset release, bootstrapped confidence intervals, 16 trials on AIME, and human validation of panic/self-doubt labels.
Limitations and LLM-use disclosure are candid, including closed-source API constraints, single-round scope, and the absence of a training-based mitigation.
weaknesses: Evaluation cannot faithfully include closed-source state-of-the-art LRMs because their APIs do not expose mid-reasoning intervention; the GPT-5.4-Mini proxy is explicitly non-native and weak, limiting claims about top proprietary systems.

The update-driven dataset is generated with GPT-5 and verified by the authors; although human-verified and >80% accepted unchanged, independent verification and broader annotation-agreement evidence are limited.
Panic and self-doubt labels rely on heuristics/LLM classifiers, validated on only 50 samples each, so the reported prevalence of these pathologies carries some uncertainty.

Main experiments focus on single, useful updates and single-round prompt-response tasks; noisy, adversarial, multiple, and long-horizon agentic interruptions remain future work, limiting external validity.

The primary relative-position interruption protocol can entangle interruption timing with problem difficulty and trace length, although sentence-level and absolute-token ablations mitigate this concern.
The prompt-guidance mitigation is a training-free postfix and only partially resolves update-driven failures, especially on AIME and coding tasks, so the paper stops short of a general solution.
Presentation has minor issues such as typos, inconsistent notation/formatting, and some appendix organization problems, though the core content remains understandable.
